Brute-force protection__TRILIUM_PH_0__

Trilium limits each IP address to 10 failed sign-in attempts in 15 minutes. Once an address reaches the limit, Trilium rejects every further attempt from it, including correct ones, until the 15 minutes have passed. The sign-in page then shows __TRILIUM_PH_0__Too many login attempts__TRILIUM_PH_1__; other clients receive HTTP status 429.
The limit applies to every way of signing in with the password:
The sign-in page.
Setting up __TRILIUM_PH_0__Synchronization__TRILIUM_PH_1__ from a desktop or mobile app.
Connecting the __TRILIUM_PH_0__Web Clipper__TRILIUM_PH_1__ or the Android sender app.
Requesting a token through __TRILIUM_PH_0__ETAPI (REST API)__TRILIUM_PH_1__.
All of these count toward the same limit, and a wrong password, a wrong one-time password and a wrong recovery code each count as one failed attempt. Successful sign-ins are not counted.
The limit is per IP address, not per account, so an attacker cannot lock you out by failing to sign in from their own address. The count is kept in memory: restarting the server clears it.

Behind a reverse proxy, Trilium sees every request as coming from the proxy unless it is configured as a __TRILIUM_PH_0__Trusted proxy__TRILIUM_PH_1__. All clients then share a single limit, so a few wrong attempts from anyone block everyone.

Multi-factor authentication with TOTP

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is a security process that requires users to provide two or more verification factors to gain access to a system, application, or account. This adds an extra layer of protection beyond just using a password.

By requiring more than one verification method, MFA helps reduce the risk of unauthorized access, even if someone has obtained your password. It’s highly recommended for securing sensitive information stored in your notes.
Relationship to OpenID Connect (OIDC)__TRILIUM_PH_0__
units.context: Multi-factor authentication with TOTP > Relationship to OpenID Connect (OIDC)

These authentication providers might provide their own security features such as TOTP or passkeys.

Signing in with OpenID Connect
OpenID is a standardized way to let you log into websites using an account from another service, like Google or Authelia, to verify your identity.

When OpenID is activated, the password-based authentication in Trilium is replaced with a button that connects using your provider. This means that the configuration of __TRILIUM_PH_0__Multi-factor authentication with TOTP__TRILIUM_PH_1__ no longer takes effect, since your provider has to handle any multi-factor authentication.

When using TLS, Trilium will verify the server certificate. If verification fails (e.g., due to self-signed certificates or certain corporate proxies), you can run the Trilium client with the __TRILIUM_PH_0__ environment variable set to __TRILIUM_PH_1__:

This will disable TLS certificate verification, significantly reducing security and exposing the setup to MITM attacks. It is strongly recommended to use a valid signed server certificate. Newer Trilium versions include a script called __TRILIUM_PH_0__ for this purpose.
Conflict Resolution__TRILIUM_PH_0__

If you edit the same note on multiple instances before synchronization, Trilium resolves conflicts by retaining the newer change and discarding the older one. The older version remains accessible in __TRILIUM_PH_0__note revisions__TRILIUM_PH_1__, allowing data recovery if needed.
Hash Check__TRILIUM_PH_0__

After each synchronization, Trilium computes a hash of all synced data on both the client and the sync server. If there is a discrepancy, Trilium will automatically initiate a recovery mechanism to resolve the issue.

Mobile Frontend
Trilium has a mobile web frontend which is optimized for touch based devices - smartphones and tablets. It is activated automatically during login process based on browser detection.
Mobile frontend is limited in features compared to the full desktop version. See below for more details on this.
Layout basics__TRILIUM_PH_0__
Unlike the desktop version, the mobile version has a slightly different UI meant to better fit the constrained screens of a mobile phone.
Here is a non-exhaustive list of differences between the desktop version and the mobile one:

On a phone, the __TRILIUM_PH_0__Note Tree__TRILIUM_PH_1__ lies under the note. The __TRILIUM_PH_2__ button in the top-left of the screen slides the note away to reveal the tree, on the folder holding the note, with the note highlighted. Opening a note from the tree slides it back in.
To return to the note without opening it again, tap its title with the __TRILIUM_PH_0__ icon in the top-right of the tree, whichever folder the tree is showing.
A swipe from the left edge of the screen also reveals the tree, but the system's or the browser's back gesture can take it over, depending on the platform.

Each tab remembers whether it was showing the tree or its note, and, for a tab left on the tree, the folder the tree was showing. Switching tabs brings both back. Once the tab shows its note again, its tree goes back to the folder holding the note.

A new tab opens on the tree, at the root, with the __TRILIUM_PH_0__Workspaces__TRILIUM_PH_1__ and the __TRILIUM_PH_2__Bookmarks__TRILIUM_PH_3__, if there are any, listed above it. Tap a workspace to hoist the tab into it.

In the Android app, the system back gesture or button closes the menu or dialog on top first, then a settings page in __TRILIUM_PH_0__Options__TRILIUM_PH_1__, then slides the note away to reveal the tree, then goes up one level in the tree. At the top of the tree, it sends the app to the background.

On wider screens, such as a tablet in landscape, the note tree is displayed as a sidebar next to the note instead. There, a __TRILIUM_PH_0__ button hides and shows it, and the choice is remembered together with the left pane of the desktop version.

A note with children shows a __TRILIUM_PH_0__ (on iOS, preceded by how many children it lists): tapping it lists its children, and tapping any other note opens it. The note whose children are listed stands at the top, with a preview of its content; tap it, or the __TRILIUM_PH_1__Open__TRILIUM_PH_2__ at its foot, to open it.
Press and hold a note to display the __TRILIUM_PH_0__Note tree contextual menu__TRILIUM_PH_1__. Opening a note in a new tab from it keeps the tree on screen, so you can open several notes in a row.
The __TRILIUM_PH_0__Quick search__TRILIUM_PH_1__ bar is also displayed at the top of the note tree.

The full __TRILIUM_PH_0__Search__TRILIUM_PH_1__ function can be triggered either from either the __TRILIUM_PH_2__Global menu__TRILIUM_PH_3__ or from the __TRILIUM_PH_4__Launch Bar__TRILIUM_PH_5__, if configured.

The __TRILIUM_PH_0__Global menu__TRILIUM_PH_1__ is shorter: __TRILIUM_PH_2__New window__TRILIUM_PH_3__ and __TRILIUM_PH_4__Keyboard shortcuts__TRILIUM_PH_5__ are left out, and __TRILIUM_PH_6__Switch to desktop version__TRILIUM_PH_7__ is under __TRILIUM_PH_8__Advanced__TRILIUM_PH_9__.
The __TRILIUM_PH_0__Launch Bar__TRILIUM_PH_1__ is displayed at the bottom of the screen.
The launch bar uses a different configuration for icons than the desktop version. See the dedicated page for more information on how to configure it.
Most of the note-related actions are grouped in the horizontal dots icon on the top-right of the note.

The __TRILIUM_PH_0__Right Sidebar__TRILIUM_PH_1__ is replaced by the note panel, a sheet that opens from the bottom of the screen with the __TRILIUM_PH_2__ button to the left of those dots. Its tabs (outline, attributes, connections, AI chat and widgets) are switched from a bar at the bottom of the sheet.
In a text note, the formatting toolbar sits at the bottom of the screen. See __TRILIUM_PH_0__Editing text notes__TRILIUM_PH_1__ below.

On iOS, the buttons of the title row, the launch bar, the formatting toolbar, the menus that open from the bottom of the screen and short dialogs are translucent panes that float clear of the screen's edges, and the note scrolls beneath the title row and the launch bar. A dialog taller than half the screen is opaque and attached to the bottom of the screen instead. To make the panes opaque, go to __TRILIUM_PH_0__Options__TRILIUM_PH_1__ → __TRILIUM_PH_2__Appearance__TRILIUM_PH_3__ → __TRILIUM_PH_4__Performance__TRILIUM_PH_5__ and turn off __TRILIUM_PH_6__Background effects for menus, popups and panels__TRILIUM_PH_7__. While the on-screen keyboard is open, a __TRILIUM_PH_0__ button in the bottom-right corner, just above the keyboard, hides it. In a text note, the button is at the right end of the formatting toolbar. While a menu of the formatting toolbar is open in place of the keyboard, the button becomes a __TRILIUM_PH_1__, which closes the menu and brings the keyboard back. The __TRILIUM_PH_0__Tabs__TRILIUM_PH_1__ are grouped under a tab switcher in the __TRILIUM_PH_2__Launch Bar__TRILIUM_PH_3__, where the tabs are displayed in a full-screen grid with preview for easy switching, as well as additional options such as reopening closed tabs. units.source: Backup encryption__TRILIUM_PH_0__

Trilium can secure the entire content of the database backup, ensuring it remains unreadable unless the correct password is provided. This is particularly useful for storing backups in unsecured locations, like network shares, unencrypted external drives, or cloud services.

Encrypted database backups use the Trilium Backup Container (.tnbackup) format, which relies on AES-256-GCM. This authenticated encryption mode scrambles the data and generates a tag confirming it hasn't been altered. The password itself isn't directly used as the key; it's processed through scrypt, a key derivation function designed to be slow and memory-intensive, making brute-force password guessing difficult even with powerful hardware. Each backup also receives a random 16-byte salt, ensuring that the same password never produces the same encryption key twice. Additionally, critical metadata such as chunk order, length, and header flags are cryptographically bound into the encryption (via "additional authenticated data"), preventing undetected tampering like reorder, truncate, or splice operations.

units.source: Backup compression__TRILIUM_PH_0__

Database backups can be optionally compressed to minimize storage footprint. This method is effective primarily when the database consists largely of text content. However, media files (images, videos, audio), along with PDF, ODF, and DOCX files, are already compressed in their original formats and won't benefit from further compression.
Compressed backups are stored using the Trilium Backup Container (.tnbackup), employing RFC 1952 GZIP compression.

__TRILIUM_PH_0__Note:__TRILIUM_PH_1__ Compression increases the time required for backup creation and restoration. It may also lead to higher CPU usage during automatic backups, potentially draining the battery faster on battery-powered devices. Enable this option only if necessary.
